q: During one complete cycle of an alternating voltage, its phase changes by:
x: One full cycle of an alternating quantity corresponds to a phase change of 2π rad, or 360°, after which the values repeat.

q: An alternating voltage is given by v = 100 sin(100πt) volts. Its frequency is:
x: Compare with v = V₀ sin ωt: ω = 100π rad s⁻¹ = 2πf, so f = 100π/2π = 50 Hz.

q: An alternating voltage v = V₀ sin ωt starts from zero at t = 0. At t = T/4, where T is its period, its phase and value are:
o: π/2, with v at its peak value V₀
π, with v back to zero
π/4, with v equal to half of V₀
2π, with v at its negative peak
x: Phase ωt = (2π/T)(T/4) = π/2, and sin(π/2) = 1, so the voltage is at its peak V₀.

q: Two alternating quantities of the same frequency are said to be in phase when they:
o: Reach their maximum and zero values at the same instants
Are produced by the same generator
x: Being in phase means a zero phase difference: both pass through zero and reach their peaks together. Equal peak values are not required.

q: In a pure inductor, the current lags behind the applied voltage because:
o: The inductor stores charge on its turns
The inductor's resistance rises with current
The self-induced back emf opposes every change in the current
The magnetic field leaks out of the coil
x: Any change in current induces a back emf that opposes it, so the current builds up a quarter-cycle after the voltage.

q: In a pure capacitor connected to AC, the current leads the voltage because:
o: The capacitor produces a back emf
The capacitor has very high resistance
The dielectric slows down the electrons
Charge must flow onto the plates before the voltage across them can build up
x: The voltage across a capacitor is V = Q/C, so it rises only after charge has flowed. The current is therefore a quarter-cycle ahead.

q: On a 50 Hz mains supply, the current in a circuit reaches its peak 2.5 ms after the voltage does. The phase lag of the current is:
x: T = 1/50 = 20 ms. A delay of 2.5 ms is 2.5/20 = 1/8 of a cycle, and 1/8 × 360° = 45°.

q: The SI unit of capacitive and inductive reactance is the:
x: Reactance is an opposition to AC, V/I, like resistance, so it is measured in ohms. The farad and henry are units of capacitance and inductance.

q: A capacitor of (250/π) μF is connected to a 50 Hz supply. Its reactance Xc = 1/(2πfC) is:
x: 2πfC = 2π × 50 × 250 × 10⁻⁶/π = 0.025, so Xc = 1/0.025 = 40 Ω. Forgetting to take the reciprocal gives 0.025.

q: A coil of inductance (0.2/π) H and negligible resistance is used on a 50 Hz supply. Its reactance XL = 2πfL is:
A 110 Ω resistor is connected to a 220 V (rms) AC supply. The rms current through it is:
x: For a resistor, Ohm's law applies to rms values: I = V/R = 220/110 = 2 A, in phase with the voltage.

q: Keeping the supply voltage fixed, the frequency applied to an ideal coil is raised to twice its value. The current it carries:
x: XL = 2πfL, so doubling f doubles the reactance. With fixed voltage, I = V/XL falls to half.

q: A capacitor in a circuit lets an alternating current flow but not a steady direct current. This is because with AC the capacitor:
o: Charges and discharges repeatedly, so charge keeps moving in the circuit
Lets electrons pass through its insulating layer
Has zero reactance at every frequency
x: No charge crosses the dielectric. With AC the plates are charged and discharged each half-cycle, so current flows in the wires; with steady DC it stops once charged.

q: An inductor of (1/π) H has a reactance of 200 Ω. The frequency of the supply is:
Which electromagnetic waves have the longest wavelength?
x: Radio waves lie at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the electromagnetic spectrum; gamma rays are at the other end.

q: Warm bodies emit a radiation that is used in TV remote controls and thermal imaging cameras. This radiation is:
x: Infrared is emitted by warm objects and is used in remote controls and thermal imaging. Ultraviolet comes mainly from very hot sources such as the Sun.

q: An electromagnetic wave in a vacuum has a frequency of 1.5 × 10⁸ Hz (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Its wavelength and its region of the spectrum are:
x: λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/(1.5 × 10⁸) = 2 m, which lies in the radio-wave region. Infrared has wavelengths below a millimetre, and dividing f by c gives 0.5 m instead.

q: Which radiation from the Sun causes sunburn and is also used to sterilise surfaces in hospitals?
x: Ultraviolet radiation damages skin cells (sunburn) and kills bacteria, so UV lamps are used for sterilisation.

q: An electromagnetic wave consists of:
o: Electric and magnetic fields oscillating along the direction of travel
Particles of matter vibrating in a medium
Electric and magnetic fields oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel
A magnetic field alone, oscillating at right angles to its motion
x: EM waves are transverse: the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, and need no medium.

q: In the electromagnetic spectrum, microwaves lie between:
x: In order of decreasing wavelength the spectrum runs radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

q: Two electromagnetic waves in a vacuum have frequencies 10¹⁵ Hz and 10¹⁸ Hz. The ratio of the wavelength of the first to that of the second is:
x: All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum, so λ = c/f and λ₁/λ₂ = f₂/f₁ = 10¹⁸/10¹⁵ = 1000.
